rv.q: In this beautifully engineered, intensely acted production, that distance becomes not merely tragic but theatrical.
This incarnation of The Pass reveals it to be a thrilling psychological drama with searing performances that has been given a vigorous presentation.
Audiences looking for a bit of eye candy won’t be disappointed by this sincere yet somewhat dated look at the travails of closeted athletes in the early part of this century.
It’s a magnetic performance well-suited to Max Hunter’s staging, which opts for exclamation points over question marks and successfully brings the play into 2026.
It's a tricky piece, irritating at first, then finding its stride in the middle before an only semi-satisfactory windup.
But “The Pass” is something of a tease — sexy, twisty, suspenseful, but also downbeat and misleading.
The Pass builds and builds, but the play falls apart before it can burst.
But director Max Hunter’s new production (the U.S. premiere) does not bring out the nuance in the material.

For those willing to enter its claustrophobic hotel rooms, the play offers a provocative glimpse into the pressures of masculinity, sexuality and celebrity—and the steep price of maintaining a carefully constructed public image.
Despite a slick production and some fantastic actors, however, this production suffers from a few key flaws that spoil the overall effect.
The Pass has momentary bursts of action and energy, but ultimately drags on like one of those scoreless matches in a Tier 21 league.

cn.t: Donnelly's drama about a closeted footballer receives mixed reviews, with critics praising its provocative themes but faulting uneven execution and a lack of nuance that prevents it from fully delivering on its promising setup.

vr.q: I enjoyed how the piece unfolded as a character study, but the road was bumpy.
